hints: Think about what the word monodentate means in terms of number of donor atoms, and what a ligand must donate to a metal.
walkthrough:
Picture what a ligand does**
Imagine $:\text{PH}_3$ approaching a metal ion. The P atom has one lone pair shown by the colon. That lone pair is donated into a vacant orbital on the metal to make a coordinate bond where both electrons come from the ligand.

Add the meaning of mono**
Mono means one. So a monodentate ligand uses only one donor atom and forms only one such coordinate bond per ligand. $:\text{PH}_3$ bonds through P only, $:\text{CO}$ bonds through C only.
Final answer: A ligand that donates one lone pair to form one coordinate (dative covalent) bond to a central metal atom or ion.

hints: Focus on the two essential components of a complex, the centre and what is attached to it.
walkthrough:
Build the picture of a complex**
Start with a transition metal ion such as $\text{Ni}^{2+}$ or $\text{Rh}^{+}$ at the centre. Then surround it with molecules or ions like $\text{NH}_3$, $\text{Cl}^-$, $\text{CO}$ that each donate a lone pair.

Name the assembly correctly**
When that central metal atom or ion is bonded to one or more ligands, the whole assembly is called a transition element complex, for example $[\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$.
Final answer: A central transition metal atom or ion bonded to one or more ligands by coordinate bonds.

hints: Consider what electronic feature transition metal ions have that allows them to accept lone pairs from ligands.
walkthrough:
Link ligands to empty orbitals**
A ligand wants to donate a lone pair, so the metal must have an empty orbital of suitable energy to receive it. Think of it as a lone pair looking for a vacant parking space.

Why transition metals are special**
Transition metal atoms and ions have partially filled d subshells with vacant d-orbitals that are low in energy and readily accessible. That is why they so easily accept lone pairs and form stable coordinate bonds to make complexes.
Final answer: Transition metal ions have vacant, energetically accessible (low lying) d-orbitals to accept lone pairs from ligands.

hints: Count the total number of coordinate bonds in each complex, remembering en is bidentate and dien is tridentate.
walkthrough:
Count bonds to get coordination number**
For $[\text{Rh}(en)_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$, each $en$ forms 2 bonds, so $2 \times 2 + 2 = 6$ bonds. For $[\text{Rh}(\text{CO})_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$, each $\text{CO}$ and $\text{Cl}$ is monodentate, so $2 + 2 = 4$ bonds. For $[\text{Au}(dien)(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2\text{Cl}]^{2+}$, $dien$ forms 3 bonds, so $3 + 2 + 1 = 6$ bonds.

Translate coordination number to shape**
Coordination number 6 is almost always octahedral. Coordination number 4 with Rh, a 4d metal, is square planar here. So the order is octahedral, square planar, octahedral.
Final answer: $[\text{Rh}(en)_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$ : octahedral; $[\text{Rh}(\text{CO})_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$ : square planar; $[\text{Au}(dien)(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2\text{Cl}]^{2+}$ : octahedral.

hints: Compare the two formulae to see which ligands are lost and which replace them, keeping dien bound throughout.
walkthrough:
Spot what changes and what stays**
Both complexes contain $\text{Au}$ and one $dien$ ligand that stays bound. The first complex has $2\text{H}_2\text{O} + 1\text{Cl}$ in addition to $dien$, the second has $3\text{Cl}$. So two water ligands are replaced by two chloride ligands.

Write the balanced exchange**
Put the two Au complexes on opposite sides and balance the free ligands: $$[\text{Au}(dien)(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2\text{Cl}]^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow [\text{Au}(dien)\text{Cl}_3] + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$$ Charge balances, $2+ + 2(-1) = 0$, and atoms balance. The reverse equation is equally correct.

hints: Recall the complex is octahedral and the three N atoms of dien all lie in the same plane around Au.
walkthrough:
Place dien first**
Draw Au at the centre of an octahedron. The $dien$ ligand, shown as N-N-N linked, is tridentate and all three N to Au bonds lie in the same plane. A common way is N at top, N at left, N at bottom, all joined by arcs.

Fill the other three sites with Cl**
An octahedron has six sites, so three remain for $\text{Cl}$. Place them to complete the octahedron, for example one to the right in the plane, one on a solid wedge out of the plane and one on a dashed wedge into the plane. Label each as Cl to give $\text{Au}(dien)\text{Cl}_3$.

Final answer: Octahedral Au with tridentate dien occupying three positions in one plane (e.g. top, left and bottom) and three $\text{Cl}$ ligands occupying the remaining three octahedral positions, drawn with solid, wedged and dashed bonds to show 3D shape: $\text{Au}(dien)\text{Cl}_3$.

hints: Use the fact that this 4-coordinate Ni complex shows no isomerism to decide between square planar and tetrahedral.
walkthrough:
Choose the correct 4-coordinate shape**
$\text{Ni}(\text{PH}_3)_2\text{Cl}_2$ has coordination number 4. Square planar $\text{MA}_2\text{B}_2$ would show cis-trans isomerism, but Table 6.1 says no isomerism is shown. That points to tetrahedral, where the two arrangements are identical.

Sketch the tetrahedron**
Put Ni at the centre. Draw two $\text{PH}_3$ ligands with normal lines and two $\text{Cl}$ ligands with one solid wedge coming out and one dashed wedge going back. That wedge-dash pair is the standard way to show a tetrahedral 3D shape.

Final answer: Tetrahedral Ni centre bonded to two $\text{PH}_3$ and two $\text{Cl}$ ligands arranged tetrahedrally, with wedge and dashed bonds to show 3D, e.g. one $\text{Cl}$ on a wedge and one $\text{Cl}$ on a dash.

hints: Think about which complex can have both cis-trans isomerism and a non-superimposable mirror image due to bidentate ligands.
walkthrough:
Compare monodentate versus bidentate cases**
$[\text{Rh}(\text{CO})_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$ has only monodentate ligands in a square plane. It shows only cis and trans, two forms. It cannot show optical isomerism.

See why the en complex gives three forms**
$[\text{Rh}(en)_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$ is octahedral with two bidentate $en$ ligands. It has trans and cis geometric isomers, and the cis form is chiral with two optical isomers that are mirror images. That makes $1 + 2 = 3$ forms in total.
Final answer: $[\text{Rh}(en)_2\text{Cl}_2]^+$ shows optical isomerism and cis-trans (geometric) isomerism, giving three isomeric forms in total.

hints: Decide the coordination number of [Ni(H2O)2(NH3)4]2+ and where the two identical H2O ligands can sit relative to each other.
Remember to label the isomer type where the two H2O ligands are at 90 degrees versus 180 degrees to each other.
walkthrough:
Draw the trans isomer**
Coordination number is $4 + 2 = 6$, so octahedral. Put Ni at the centre. For trans, place the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands opposite, one straight up and one straight down. Fill the four equatorial positions with $\text{NH}_3$, using wedge and dash for the out of plane pair.

Draw the cis isomer and name the type**
For cis, place the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands next to each other at 90 degrees, for example one up and one to the right. Fill the remaining four sites with $\text{NH}_3$. Because the difference is only the positions of ligands around the metal, this is cis-trans or geometric isomerism.

Final answer: Two octahedral structures of $[\text{Ni}(\text{NH}_3)_4(\text{H}_2\text{O})_2]^{2+}$: one trans isomer with the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands opposite each other (180 degrees) and one cis isomer with the two $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ ligands adjacent (90 degrees), $\text{NH}_3$ ligands filling the other four sites with wedge/dash bonds shown. Type: cis-trans (geometric) isomerism.
